intro: Rachmaninoff turns a polka his father liked to play into a small keyboard comedy: the tune keeps its dancing bass while the hands grow ever busier around it. This is the composer’s 1919 Edison recording.

sections.label: A · A tune over the polka bass
sections.mNote: Allegretto; bass notes alternate with light chords

sections.label: B · Faster, with staccato chords
sections.mNote: Poco più mosso; both hands play accented chords

sections.label: C · The dance slows and wanders
sections.mNote: Meno mosso; a slurred melody over left-hand chords

sections.label: D · Scherzando in E major
sections.mNote: The tune turns up in a new key

sections.label: A′ · The A♭ tune returns
sections.mNote: Tempo I; the opening dance gains a countermelody

sections.label: Coda · A quiet final bow
sections.mNote: Meno mosso, ritardando and a last pp chord

cues.title: The bass starts dancing
cues.text: A few bars of semiquavers slow and fade before the tune arrives at pp. The left hand alternates a bass note with a chord: the polka’s oom-pah. Above it, the right hand slips little triplets between the melody notes.
cues.evidence: Piano Street score, p. 1: Allegretto, diminuendo and ritardando before the pp tune and alternating bass notes and chords. https://www.pianostreet.com/rachmaninoff-sheet-music/polka-de-w-r.htm
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: His father’s favourite polka
cues.text: Vasily Rachmaninoff likes to play this tune, and his son gives the arrangement his father’s initials. The melody belongs to Franz Behr’s Scherzpolka, Op. 303. Rachmaninoff moves it from F to A♭ major and dedicates his 1911 version to Leopold Godowsky.
cues.evidence: Jeremy Nicholas’s notes for Hyperion identify Vasily, Behr’s Op. 303, the transposition, the 1911 arrangement and the Godowsky dedication. https://www.hyperion-records.co.uk/dw.asp?dc=W5662_GBAJY9148612

cues.title: The dance catches its breath
cues.text: Meno mosso slows the dance after the staccato chords. A slurred melody curls over left-hand chords; a tempo restores the pace, then another Meno mosso holds it back. Rachmaninoff keeps changing his mind about how quickly to go.
cues.evidence: Piano Street score, pp. 3–4: ritardando, Meno mosso and repeated alternations with a tempo.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Ten sides for Edison
cues.text: In April 1919 Rachmaninoff, newly arrived in America and in need of money, agrees to record for Edison. Edison wants ten sides at once, before any contract is signed, and issues all three takes of each. The RCA booklet that reissues them calls the sound “distant and disappointing”.
cues.evidence: RCA/BMG booklet to the 10-CD Complete Recordings (09026 61265 2, 1992), essay “The Recordings”, p. 28: the April 1919 Edison contract, the ten sides, three takes of each all issued, and the phrase “distant and disappointing”. https://archive.org/details/9-0023-sergei-rachmaninoff-complete-recordings-booklet-to-10-cd-set-rca-bmg-09026-61265-2-1992

cues.title: A joke in E major
cues.text: The tune turns up in E major, marked scherzando — playfully. Short accented chords and quick inner notes jostle against the bass. The change from four flats to four sharps makes a new corner of the keyboard feel like home.
cues.evidence: Piano Street score, pp. 4–5: change to four sharps and Tempo precedente, scherzando; E major harmony at the new section.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Two tunes in A♭
cues.text: A♭ major returns with the opening tempo. Rachmaninoff adds his own countermelody to Behr’s tune, giving the little dance another voice. The hands have more to say even while the bass keeps its familiar step.
cues.evidence: Piano Street score, p. 5, Tempo I and continuation; Jeremy Nicholas’s Hyperion notes identify the new countermelody accompanying the main theme’s return.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The last soft chord
cues.text: A quiet run climbs through the high notes. Meno mosso and a ritardando slow the final bars, and the piece ends on a soft chord under a fermata. The polka takes a small bow.
cues.evidence: Piano Street score, p. 8, final system: pp rising run, Meno mosso, ritardando and final pp chord with fermata.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: Both hands strike short chords
transitions.from: A · A tune over the polka bass
transitions.how: Poco più mosso quickens the dance. In A♭ major, both hands play short, accented chords, beginning at mf and growing through f to ff. Rests cut the chord pairs apart while the bass keeps leaping.
transitions.evidence: Piano Street score, p. 3: Poco più mosso, staccato chords, crescendo, f and ff.

transitions.title: A run softens the chords
transitions.to: C · The dance slows and wanders
transitions.how: A descending right-hand figure and a ritardando draw the music away from the ff chords. At Meno mosso, the right hand plays a slurred melody above moving inner notes and a held left-hand chord. The marking drops to mf.
transitions.evidence: Piano Street score, p. 3, final two systems: descending figure, ritardando and Meno mosso at mf.

transitions.title: A quick run reaches E major
transitions.from: C · The dance slows and wanders
transitions.how: Poco a poco rallentando slows the curling melody. A run marked veloce starts softly, swells and descends; the left hand falls silent beneath its last notes. At the double bar, E major and Tempo precedente restore the dancing pace, with scherzando written above the tune.
transitions.evidence: Piano Street score, pp. 4–5: rallentando, veloce run, four-sharp key signature and Tempo precedente, scherzando.

transitions.title: Four flats and the old tune
transitions.how: The E major passage ends with a change back to four flats. Forte sextuplets sweep above left-hand broken chords, then a ritardando eases into Tempo I. The A♭ major tune returns at p, with a second melodic line running beside it.
transitions.evidence: Piano Street score, p. 5: four-flat signature, forte sextuplets, ritardando and Tempo I; the added countermelody is discussed in Jeremy Nicholas’s Hyperion notes.

transitions.title: The quick hands come to rest
transitions.how: A long pp run rises across the keyboard before Meno mosso. The left hand holds a low octave, the right hand’s line slows through a ritardando, and a final high chord completes the A♭ major ending at pp, under a fermata.
transitions.evidence: Piano Street score, p. 8, final system: pp run, Meno mosso, held bass, ritardando and the final chord.

fields.label: Work version
fields.value: Composer’s arrangement for piano (1911) of Franz Behr’s Scherzpolka Lachtäubchen, Op. 303, as played by him
fields.note: The printed title is Polka de W. R. (W. for Wassily, the composer’s father); the RCA set and the Archive file use V.R. Behr’s theme is transposed from F to A♭ with an added counter-melody and without Behr’s middle section. The score prints ossia alternatives, and the edition used by the composer for this recording is not identified.

fields.label: Recorded
fields.note: Sources agree on April 1919 and disagree on the day. The Archive filenames, the RCA register give 23 April; DAHR’s Edison ledger entry and the Classical Pianists chronology give 24 April. The day is not resolved here.

fields.label: Place
fields.note: DAHR gives New York for every take. The label place of publication, Orange, New Jersey, is not the session place.

fields.label: Label
fields.note: Edison is the original label (released at Orange, New Jersey, according to DAHR’s label record); the uploader identifies the 1992 RCA/BMG set as the immediate source of the file.

fields.label: Catalogue
fields.value: Edison Diamond Disc 82187 (10-inch double-faced; Polka on side L, Prelude in C♯ minor on side R); RCA-BMG 09026 61265 2, CD 10 (1992)
fields.note: The side assignment and disc number are documented by the Edison list and the Florida Atlantic catalogue; the disc used for the 1992 transfer is not identified. DAHR’s MARC record for the disc gives 10-inch, 80 rpm and a bracketed publication year of [1919], which predates the release documented by the National Park Service and Densmore (December 1920) and is not followed for the release date; either proposed publication year predates 1926.

fields.label: Matrix, take, sides
fields.note: The RCA register names Edison 6744-B for CD 10, track 15, and the Archive file is that track. Edison issued all three takes (A, B, C) on the same catalogue number, so the disc number alone does not identify the take, and no comparison of takes was made. DAHR gives its own take dates (24 April 1919) which differ from the RCA register (23 April).

fields.label: Transfer
fields.value: John Pfeiffer, reissue producer; Ward Marston, disc-to-DAT transfer; André Gauthier, remastering supervisor; Anthony Salvatore, remastering engineer
fields.note: These are the credits printed for the 1992 RCA/BMG set. Their connection to this access file rests on the uploader’s identification of the item as CD 10 of that set. The later ripper and uploader are not named as engineers.

fields.label: Transfer date
fields.note: The set was issued in 1992, but the dates of the disc-to-DAT transfer, the remastering and the later CD extraction are not stated. The Internet Archive upload of 11 October 2025 is not a transfer date.

fields.label: Processing
fields.value: Disc-to-DAT transfer, then digital remastering at BMG/RCA Studios, New York City; the Internet Archive derives its VBR MP3 from an uploaded WAV.
fields.note: The booklet says surface imperfections were reduced without radical removal of all surface noise. It gives no equalisation, pitch-correction, noise-reduction or editing settings, and none is inferred from the audio analysis. The booklet’s essay says the Edison engineer evidently placed the upright piano too far from the recording horns, so the sound is distant.

fields.label: Composition rights
fields.value: Underlying composition is out of copyright where the ordinary life-plus-70 term applies.
fields.note: Rachmaninoff died in 1943. This is a territorial term calculation, not worldwide clearance or a statement about any modern edition. Franz Behr died in 1898, so the underlying polka is also out of copyright on the same calculation.

fields.label: Recording rights
fields.value: US public domain: the issued sound recording was published by 1925 (Edison Diamond Disc 82187, released December 1920).
fields.note: The National Park Service catalogue and Densmore’s list both give a December 1920 release for Edison 82187, whose side L carries the Polka; this is independent of the April 1919 session date. The Archive item’s Public Domain Mark is noted but not relied on. The 1992 booklet carries an all-rights-reserved reissue notice: no claim is made that its text, artwork or compilation is public domain, or that any new creative contribution to the mastering is cleared worldwide.

composer.epithet: In exile he earned his living at the piano, while the bells of his Russian childhood kept sounding through the music he wrote.
facts: Zverev and Siloti at the piano; Taneyev and Arensky in composition
Ivanovka, Dresden, New York, Villa Senar and Beverly Hills
Four piano concertos, three symphonies, three completed operas, choral music, songs and piano works

quote.text: I feel like a ghost wandering in a world grown alien. I cannot cast out the old way of writing, and I cannot acquire the new.
quote.source: Rachmaninoff to Leonard Liebling, 1939; published in The Musical Courier, 5 April 1943

composer.background:
“My hearty thanks to the old man for not having forgotten about me!” Rachmaninoff wrote to the singer Mikhail Slonov on 26 December 1892. The old man was Tchaikovsky, who had praised his opera Aleko in a newspaper interview. Rachmaninoff was nineteen, newly graduated from the Moscow Conservatory with its Great Gold Medal. Tchaikovsky helped get the opera into the Bolshoi, and in May 1893 sat in the audience applauding. For a young composer, it was an excellent beginning.

His childhood had been less orderly. Born into a landowning family, he grew up at Oneg, near Novgorod, until his father’s financial failures forced a move to St Petersburg. He entered the Conservatory there in 1883. His parents separated; his sister Sofia died of diphtheria; schoolwork went badly. His grandmother took him to Orthodox services, where he heard the voices and bells that would stay with him. In 1885 his cousin Alexander Siloti recommended a move to Moscow, under the formidable care of the piano teacher Nikolai Zverev.
